newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Nablus blockade lifted, but no shoppers arrive.
newsitem.headline: Nablus blockade lifted, but no shoppers arrive.

text.p: Few Palestinians arrived to the business capital of the West Bank to shop on Wednesday as Israel flung open the gates of PLO-ruled Nablus after a 20-day blockade.
Businessmen complained of "very slow" activity after the Jewish state eased travel restrictions imposed on Nablus last month during fierce gun battles between Palestinians and Israeli troops.
The streets were nearly deserted on Wednesday and markets saw little activity.
"This is the worst slow down that I have ever seen," said a wholesale grocery merchant, waiting for customers to enter his store.

"Even during the intifada, we were opening for business for only a few hours a day but we used to sell," he said, referring to a Palestinian uprising which began in 1987 and lasted until a 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal was reached.
Israel imposed travel restrictions on seven PLO-ruled West Bank cities on September 26, one day after unprecedented clashes erupted in which 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed.
Nablus was the scene of some of the bloodiest fighting. Six Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed when Palestinians overran an army position at an Israeli-held shrine in the town.
Israel lifted the blockade on most of the West Bank last week but kept Nablus closed until Wednesday, prompting speculation that the Jewish state was taking revenge for the casualties.
The blockade cut off more than 3,500 Palestinians in the Nablus district from work in Israel and stifled commerce, industry and agriculture.
Factory owners said they were working at less than 30 percent capacity because of the absense of workers, lack of raw materials and inability to export products.

"People did not earn any income during the past 20 days and if you don't have money, you cannot buy and sell," Basel Kanaan, a businessman and member of the board of the Nablus Chamber of Commerce told Reuters.
Samir Hijjawi, a jeweller who returned from the Gulf in 1994 hoping to benefit from peace dividends, said he had no customers all day.
"The situation is very frustrating. I brought my life savings from the Gulf and returned hoping to help rebuild my country. I was hopeful but now I am pessimistic," he said.
